title: STRANGE MINUTE #17 · WHAT IF

lines.text: What if Earth had rings like Saturn?
Some scientists think it really did, 466 million years ago.
lines.say: Some scientists think it really did, four hundred sixty-six million years ago.

lines.text: Saturn's rings stretch 175,000 miles, but they're only about 30 feet thick.
lines.say: Saturn's rings stretch a hundred seventy-five thousand miles, but they're only about thirty feet thick.

lines.text: Stand on the equator, and you'd see a thin line cut the sky in half.
Farther north, it becomes a giant arch across the sky.
At night, sunlit rings would make the dark glow.
But in winter, their shadow falls on half the planet.
Every rocket launch would have to dodge ring debris.
And chunks would keep falling as meteors.
So, would you trade warm winters for a ring in the sky?

sources: Monash University 2024 (Tomkins et al., Earth and Planetary Science Letters): Earth may have had a ring ~466 million years ago (21 Ordovician craters within 30° of the equator); hypothesis, debated
NASA/JPL: Saturn's ring system extends up to 175,000 miles (282,000 km); about 30 feet (10 m) thick in most places
Ring plane over the equator; seasonal ring shadow on the winter hemisphere (standard geometry; Monash authors speculate shading/cooling)
